name: Dana Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior shepherd at High Fell, which is a hill farm, steep rough grazing up to about six hundred metres, with eleven hundred ewes. Right now the rams are in with the ewes, so most mornings I'm on the quad bike with Moss, my dog, checking which ewes have been marked by the crayon on the ram's chest. Afternoons it's fencing, foot trimming, or carrying feed blocks up to the top ground.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the gathering days, when we bring the whole hill down with four dogs and you can see the flock pouring off the slope like water. What wears me out is the weather. Sideways rain for a week, and you're soaked to your underwear by nine. Also, I'm honestly not good enough with the dogs yet. Moss is better at this job than I am.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Loads, more than the boss, Alan. I keep the lambing records in an app on my phone, I ask a chatbot when I'm not sure about a sick ewe before I ring the vet, and I've been reading about virtual fencing collars, GPS collars that keep sheep in an area with sound instead of a wire fence. Alan thinks I'm a bit mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's great, honestly, and I'd say it on the farming groups I'm in online. It already saves me ringing the vet for every limping ewe. That's money for Alan and a bit of confidence for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I stay where I am, poor and happy. I've got about two weeks of money saved. My partner Jo works at the outdoor centre down the valley, seasonal, so in winter we're tight. A better search engine doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it, push Alan to let me try the virtual fencing on one block of ground. Apply for the young farmers' grant scheme for a bit of training. Learn the dogs properly, which no app can do for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit restless, maybe, because I want things to move faster than they do up here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the farm's biggest problem that a tool like that couldn't touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. Hill sheep barely pay. A good ewe lamb sells for less than her keep some years, and the farm lives on the public payments for looking after the land. If those got cut, no app saves us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dogs are something no app can do. Tell me about a time that showed you that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last September I sent Moss the wrong way round a group and pushed forty ewes straight into a bog. Alan didn't shout, he just whistled her back and sorted it in two minutes. You can't read that off a screen. It's in your whistle and your feet.

S0.say: I'd say it's great, and I'd say so on my online farming groups. It already saves me ringing the vet for every limping ewe, which saves Alan money.
S0.think: Privately it means I stay where I am, poor and happy. I've got about two weeks of money, and Jo's seasonal job means winter is always tight.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily and pushes Alan to trial virtual fencing collars on one block of ground. Applies for a young farmers' training grant and works on handling the dogs properly.
S0.feel: Calm, with a restless edge because she wants change to come faster.
S0.quote: You can't read that off a screen. It's in your whistle and your feet.
S0.fieldNote: The most enthusiastic user of AI tools in this group, yet the story she chose to tell was about a skill no tool can give her. She's clear that hill farming lives on public payments, which frames her politics. Upbeat but aware she's poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for young people, and that farming needs beginners more than most jobs. Nobody my age is coming into hill sheep. If farms hire even fewer of us, the hills just go back to bracken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Secretly I think I'd be fine, maybe better off. If it's slow, I've got ten years to become the person on the hill who knows the collars and the drones and the records. Alan's sixty-one. When he stops, somebody's got to run this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build up my skills on the tech side so I'm worth keeping. Try to get a small drone licence, because people already use drones to check sheep on steep ground. And I'd ask Alan straight out whether he'd consider me as the tenant when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Slow change is the kind I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Alan go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, the first time. He'd laugh and say I can't even work Moss yet. But he'd think about it on the quad on the way home. That's how he is. Nothing gets decided at the table, it gets decided on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer young people coming in is a shame, but also that you might be better off. How do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't really. Less competition is good for me and bad for the valley. I can hold both. I'd still rather there were ten of us than just me.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for young people, because hill farming needs beginners more than most jobs. If farms hire fewer of us, the hills just go back to bracken.
S1.think: Secretly I think I'd be fine, maybe better off. Slow change gives me ten years to become the person who knows the collars, drones and records, and Alan is sixty-one.
S1.do: Builds tech skills and gets a small drone licence for checking sheep on steep ground. Asks Alan directly whether he'd consider her as tenant when he retires.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, because slow change suits her.
S1.quote: Nothing gets decided at the table, it gets decided on the hill.
S1.fieldNote: She sees opportunity where most of her peers in this group see threat, and named the retirement gap plainly. She admitted the contradiction between valuing more young farmers and benefiting from fewer. Her plan is specific: drone licence, then the tenancy question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office workers need protecting, and I'd say it loudly. I'd back a tax on companies that cut staff with AI, and I'd want that money going into rural jobs too. Hill farms look after the water and the peat for the whole country, that's a public job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it might help me. If there are new AI-related jobs, maybe some of them are things like running the land data for the public payments. That's paperwork Alan hates, and an assistant that does it with me could save the farm a week a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the assistant doing our paperwork for the land scheme by the spring. I'd try to make a bit of side money helping other hill farmers set theirs up, maybe a few at forty or fifty a go. I'd join the young farmers' policy group, because when politicians argue, you want somebody from the hills in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Jo's friends in town who work in offices. Quite good about my own patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could helping other farmers with paperwork turn into a real income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few hundred a year, which for us is a lot. Not a career. But it gets my name known in the valley, and that matters if I want a tenancy one day. People trust the person who sorted their forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister. She's in a call centre in the city, answering bank questions. She'd be first out. I'd have her on the sofa in a month, and Jo would be lovely about it, but our place is tiny.

S2.say: I'd say office workers need protecting and back a tax on companies that cut staff with AI. Some of that money should go to rural jobs, because hill farms look after the water and peat for everyone.
S2.think: Honestly I think it might help me. New AI jobs could include running the land data for public payments, which Alan hates, and an assistant could save the farm a week a year.
S2.do: Sets up an AI assistant for the farm's land scheme paperwork by spring. Offers the same help to other hill farmers for forty or fifty each, and joins the young farmers' policy group.
S2.feel: Uneasy for friends and her sister in office jobs, fairly positive about her own situation.
S2.quote: People trust the person who sorted their forms.
S2.fieldNote: She turns a threat to others into a small business idea within minutes, and ties it back to her long-term goal of a tenancy. Her progressive politics have a rural edge: public money for public goods. Her real worry is her sister in a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry in public. House prices booming means the valley fills up with second homes and holiday lets, and people like me get pushed out. I'd be at every meeting saying the gains should pay for affordable rural housing and land for new farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's safe and my life isn't. We rent a converted barn off a man who'd sell it tomorrow for double. And if rich people flood in looking for country land, Alan's farm is worth more as a rich person's estate than as sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a savings plan, even small, fifty a month, which hurts. I'd talk to the land trust in the valley about their starter farm scheme. And my sister would definitely be on our sofa, so I'd try to get her work at the outdoor centre with Jo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The work is fine and the ground under it is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo the night the landlord said he was selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll go to my mum's in town for a bit, which neither of us wants. Then I'd lie awake doing sums. I'd probably ask a chatbot what our rights are, at two in the morning, because that's what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still feel you could stay in hill farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but maybe not on this hill. There are schemes, co-ops, people renting small bits of land together. I'd go anywhere with sheep. I just wouldn't want to watch High Fell turn into a shooting estate.

S3.say: I'd be angry in public and say the gains should pay for affordable rural housing and land for new farmers. Booming house prices fill the valley with second homes and push people like me out.
S3.think: My job's safe and my life isn't. Our landlord would sell our barn tomorrow for double, and Alan's farm would be worth more as a rich person's estate than as sheep.
S3.do: Starts saving fifty a month and contacts the valley land trust about its starter farm scheme. Takes in her sister and tries to get her work at the outdoor centre alongside Jo.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the work is steady while everything underneath it shifts.
S3.quote: My job's safe and my life isn't.
S3.fieldNote: Like others in this group, the housing boom worried her more than job loss. She was ready to leave this hill for any hill, which shows how strong her attachment is to the work itself. The two-in-the-morning chatbot detail rang very true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on flat arable land, sure, but put one on our hill in January and see what happens. I'd also say, if robots are coming to farms, workers should share in the gains, not just landowners. I'd be pushing for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think they'd come for the hill too, just later. Drones are already doing a good bit of what I do on the quad. A robot dog that can climb a steep hillside, with a camera that spots a lame ewe, that's not science fiction, I've seen the videos. A robot can't read a ewe's face at three in the morning. Not yet. And I'd rather be the one teaching it than the one it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to be first. Ask Alan to let me trial whatever comes, even pay part of the cost back from my wages if it meant I was the one running it. Get every certificate going. And I'd keep Moss, robot or not, because she's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and excited at once. It's a bit like the top of a steep gather, you can't see the bottom but you're going down anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay part of the cost from your wages, with two weeks of savings. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. It's what I'd offer, and Alan would say no because he knows what I earn. But offering is the point. It says I'm in, don't replace me with the thing, give me the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else do you think would lose out on the hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shearers. Contract gangs that go farm to farm in summer. If someone builds a shearing robot, that's a whole way of life gone, and those men have nothing else. I'd feel worse for them than for me.

S4.say: I'd say robots might work on flat arable land, but not on our hill in January. If robots come to farms, workers should share in the gains, not just landowners.
S4.think: Privately I think robots would reach the hill too, just later, because drones already do some of my quad work. I'd rather be the one teaching the machine than the one it replaced.
S4.do: Asks Alan to let her run any trial and offers to pay part of the cost from her wages. Gets every certificate available, and keeps Moss whatever happens.
S4.feel: Anxious and excited together, like heading down a steep slope she can't see the bottom of.
S4.quote: A robot can't read a ewe's face at three in the morning. Not yet. And I'd rather be the one teaching it than the one it replaced.
S4.fieldNote: Even here she leaned in rather than back, though she admitted her offer to pay was more gesture than plan. Her 'not yet' carried real weight. She shifted her concern to contract shearers, which shows how her progressive outlook steers her attention to others.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one without robots, the third one, which surprises me. Robots I can learn. House prices I can't do anything about. What would help is land for new farmers, starter tenancies, and rented homes in the valley that can't be turned into holiday lets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Hill farms aren't just food, they're water, peat, birds. If the robots and the money all go to the flat farms, nobody looks after the hills, and that hits people in cities who've never seen a sheep.

headlineQuote: A robot can't read a ewe's face at three in the morning. Not yet. And I'd rather be the one teaching it than the one it replaced.
portrait: Dana Chen is a 27-year-old junior shepherd on a steep hill farm with eleven hundred ewes, working alongside her dog Moss and a 61-year-old boss, Alan. She uses AI tools every day, has about two weeks of savings and rents a converted barn with her partner Jo. She sees slow AI and even office automation as chances to make herself valuable and one day take on a tenancy. Her deepest fear is not robots but the housing boom in the fast scenario, which could push her out of the valley. With robots she would rather run the machines than be replaced by them, while worrying about contract shearers more than herself.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario without robots, because a housing boom could push her out of her rented home and turn hill farms into estates for the rich.
whatWouldHelp: Land and starter tenancies for new farmers, and protected rented homes in rural valleys that can't be turned into holiday lets.
